title: Subitising: See How Many at a Glance
seo_title: Foundation Subitising Worksheets: Dot Cubes, Ten-Frames and Small Groups to 5 (Free, with Answers)
standard_text: Recognise and name the number of objects within a collection up to 5 using subitising.
meta_desc: Free Foundation (Prep, Kindergarten) maths worksheets on subitising to 5, matched to the Australian Curriculum (AC9MFN02): dot cubes, ten-frames, small groups and two parts at a glance. 100 picture questions with answers.
key_big: Small groups up to 5 can be seen all at once, without counting.
key_sub: Learn the dot cube patterns. On a ten-frame, a full top row is 5. See 2 and 3 and know it is 5.
body_html:
See it without counting

Subitising means looking at a small group and knowing how many straight away, without counting one by one. Children learn to do this for groups up to 5.

Use a ten-frame

The top row of a ten-frame holds 5. If the whole top row is full, there are 5.

Two small parts

Bigger groups can be seen as two small parts: see 2 and 3, and know it is 5.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do
Guessing after a very quick lookLook at the pattern, then check by counting
Thinking spread-out things are moreSpreading out does not change how many
Counting only one partSay both parts, then how many altogether

faq.a: Subitising is seeing how many are in a small group at a glance, without counting. The Australian Curriculum (AC9MFN02) asks Foundation students to subitise collections up to 5.
It builds number sense. Children who can see 3 and 2 quickly can later see 5, add small numbers in their heads and use ten-frames.

faq.q: How can I help my child subitise at home?
faq.a: Play games with a dot cube, dominoes or playing cards. Flash a small group of blocks for a second and ask: How many did you see? How did you see it?

faq.q: Should my child still count to check?
faq.a: Yes. Seeing the amount first and then counting to check is a good habit. Over time the counting will be needed less.
